idiom_name: decorator factory over the callable, plus the framework middleware onion
implementation_notes: A gate is a decorator factory that wraps the next callable and checks before delegating, and the chain is the nesting of those wrappers; web frameworks express the same shape as a middleware onion (Django applies MIDDLEWARE top-down during the request phase and in reverse on the way out; ASGI middleware wraps the application), where any layer can short-circuit by returning a response without calling the inner one. What replaces the classic structure: higher-order functions and framework middleware lists replace proxy classes and a hand-built chain, and the verified identity belongs in the request or in a contextvars.ContextVar set by the gate - each gate must verify the artifact again rather than trust the value it finds. functools.wraps preserves the wrapped callable's identity, and an async gate must be async-aware or it returns an un-awaited coroutine instead of enforcing anything.
pitfalls: A synchronous decorator around an async view returns an un-awaited coroutine without enforcing anything; async and sync gates are separate code paths (Django requires declaring async_capable).
A layer that catches the denial and continues, or returns None on failure, fails open - exactly one handler should map the denial to 403 and every other gate should let it propagate.

Module-level mutable state (a cached identity, a shared policy) is shared across requests and workers; per-request data belongs in the request or a ContextVar, and ContextVars should be created at module level, never in closures.
